en: Was held firm by its massive weight.
Their raven eyes blazed,
They had their fine steeds tethered,
Terrifying all they threatened,
And had the racehorses saddled,
Then the two giants
Took eighty warriors from Kambyl,
Darkening with rage,
Rain falling from their fury,
Water streaming from their march,
An uproar rising at their tidings,
They prepared horses to mount with a bound,
And coats to don when refreshed,
They laid in abundant ammunition,
And had their weapons packed,
They loaded a red camel,
That could travel forty days without water,
And never once grow faint with weariness,
The equal of the swiftest riding camel,
No other beast like it existed,
Hook-nosed, with a back like a trap,
They mounted their horses in ordered ranks,
And fitted handsome harness,
They draped themselves in warriors’ coats,
The two lions Ebegey and Kögöy
Had long been making ready.
The two villains Ebegey and Kögöy
Set out to ravage the people,
Traveling for many days,
They reached great Khotan beyond Kashgar,
Made great Khotan their base,
Skirted broad Kashgar,
Encircled the Six Cities,
Watched the hill country closely,
And once again destroyed
All the fine horses of the valleys,
Brave Seytek was the one they sought,
Their hearts black as soot,
They came straight toward him.
Let us leave this matter here,
And of your heroic elder Akjoltoy,
Let us now begin the tale.
The well-built racehorse Kulunsur
Was his tethered mount,
While he lived as a hero on the people’s frontier,
In the middle of the night
He awoke with a start,
Tossing and turning anxiously,
And saddled Kulunsur,
“It has now been seven days,
And seven nights,
But forlorn Kulunsur,
My child, will not stand when I tether him,
And will not graze when I release him,
He sighs and gazes inward.
He neighs and seems to sob,
This frisking mad creature
Pounds the black earth.
Kulunsur’s appearance has changed,
His sigh can split stone,
His snort can split a head,
He was a beast grown fat on rich pasture,
And on that ill-fated racehorse
There was a handspan of flank fat,
But he has drawn in his fat and tucked up his belly,
He looks ready for battle,
The creature is meant to be ridden to war,
It is clear he is ready to race into combat.”
He hastily saddled him,
And elder Akjoltoy took alarm:
“I shall circle the face of the earth,
And seek tidings of the warriors.
Many flatter you, saying, ‘You are heroes and lions,’
Many merely wink their eyes,
Many enemies wish to strike,
Many will scatter us if they can,
Many will overrun us if they have the strength,
In many places trouble brews,
And the hateful enemy harbors designs,
To preserve our lives and survival,
There are many who would keep the plow from turning,
Keep it from opening furrows in the earth,
Not let us take one free step,
Not let us sow any crops,
Not let us live in peace,
And seek to seize all we possess,
There are many champions who would bring calamity,
Many warriors who would take lives,
Many burn with bloodlust,
Many swagger, displaying their might,
And would slaughter us and spill our blood,
May they not ravage the people, torment the nation,
And bring countless disasters!”
In urgent alarm,
He donned his battle gear,
Summoned Köygashka,
Took him as his companion,
Gathered warriors whose host cast a vast shadow,
And rode out on patrol in alarm.
Your heroic elder Joltoy was keen-eyed,
A surveyor who watched and knew
All four corners of the world.
His words were plain when he spoke,
A true seer whose eyes were open,
A warrior who had traveled among countless peoples,
A man who could distinguish
An enemy from a kinsman.
Reading an omen from his steed,
He tightened the belt around his waist,
Faced the ridge and followed the tracks,
And when he reached the crest,
Ask not how the hero fared:
He drew the strap from his back,
And took the spyglass in his hand,
At all four corners of the world
He turned and gazed intently,
Seeking tidings from the land,
Toward the blessed Besh-Moynok
The horizon was hazy,
Seeking tidings of the people,
Beyond that visible valley,
On the far side of Jangyryk,
This side of the neighboring mountain,
Joltoy stood watching.
A fearsome cloud of dust rose from the pass,
Some forty men mingled with the dust,
Riding together and loosing arrows,
Following the length of Jar-Kyya,
Swinging swords and thrusting spears,
Competing in many different feats,
Their dust crashed into dust,
And whirled in the sky,
Their bearing and their grandeur,
Their appearance on horseback
Seemed extraordinary,
Their spears bore mail pennons,
And their arts of war
Each appeared distinct.
Their horses’ necks arched like swans,
They rode beasts of many kinds,
Finding no enemy to fight,
They rode about pouring out their wrath.
A thought occurred
To your formidable elder Joltoy:
“There is a ditch left by our fathers,
There is light within darkness,
There is a refuge if one flees in fright,
And there is a saying: before an angry man,
Oh, my child, do not make a show of force.
If you seek livestock, go early,
Once twilight falls, the eye cannot see,
Head off coming strife before it arrives,
Once a quarrel starts, words cannot reach it.
I shall bring them to reason,
Fold my hands, offer them food,
And bow my head, saying, ‘Stay,’
If they heed me and submit to reason,
Let me strike with honeyed words,
If he bristles and refuses to talk,
I shall seize him by the collar.
I shall forestall the quarrel,
I shall block the violent man’s path.
Wisdom’s husbandman, Akjoltoy,
With the majesty of a vast host,
Whose every utterance was sweet,
A fluent, free-speaking servant,
A servant well prepared in speech,
In great and restless haste,
His surpassing resourcefulness revealed,
Kulunsur, huge as a bare mountain,
Sprang and ran like an arrow,
And loaded his gold upon a camel.
Kulunsur and the red camel,
To those two raging men,
To the giants Ebegey and Kögöy,
He led them forth as gifts.
Warriors, you have come
From your homeland,
You have set out from your people;
Here is the khan, and here am I,
If you advance, here lies Talas,
Here am I, the eloquent Akjoltoy!
If you truly are khans,
You will pass for lions;
If you are witless, worthless men,
If you are fools who understand no words,
You will cut off the offered head.
The red camel is the gift, and I am the sacrifice—
So your Akjoltoy spoke eloquently.
Ebegey and Kögöy, two giants,
If you two will come to your senses,
You are the ones to whom I speak,
You are my shining dark eyes.
You have stood for deeds of renown,
We are kinsmen of a single root;
If you will not heed reason or words,
You are wretches who ruin the cause.
No Chinese foe with a red-tasseled spear
Is here, shouting and thrusting;
No fearsome enemy is here
Who comes raging against us,
With a feud from ages past.
Consider where this deed will lead;
I bow my neck before what is right,
I offer all my worldly wealth.
Our roots are one, so let us unite;
Our pastures adjoin, so let us stand together.
Our faith is shared, our lives are one—
I say that we must unite.
Though we wage slaughter for forty years,
Though we raid horses with battle cries,
We are steeds that never tire.
Though slaughter lasts for forty years,
Though we clash in combat,
Though we don blood-soaked caps,
Destroying property and taking peace away,
Piercing lungs and taking heads,
Though we become bitter enemies,
We are kin who cannot endure separation.
Ebegey and Kögöy, two lions,
If you are heroes, you will understand:
No one can break the strength
Of a small people firmly united,
But everyone commands the sons
Of a numerous people without unity.
If we stand firm by our pledged word,
If we face the foe that faces us,
Can any cold-hearted invader come
Boasting and playing the hero,
And defeat us in battle?!
If divided, shall we not be overcome,
And the heroes’ backs be broken?
Will not the many enemies who hate us
Overrun and slaughter us,
Quenching the fire we have kindled,
Plundering and laying waste,
Until our battling foe is satisfied
And the heroes’ fortune is broken!
If heads are cut off, the people will be thrown into turmoil,
And the triumphant enemy will rejoice.
Ebegey and Kögöy, two lions,
Accept the livestock offered to you.
As for the weighty words just spoken,
Whether profound or shallow,
Look deeply into their meaning!—
So Akjoltoy spoke,
Folding his hands and presenting the gift,
Sharpening his precious tongue;
Your elder, the venerable Akjoltoy,
Spoke on unwaveringly.
When they witnessed this deed,
Ebegey and Kögöy, the two lions,
Lowered their banners to the ground,
And from their twin thoroughbred steeds
Leapt down and ran forward.
